caption:
A new Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ update shipped music that players traced to the AI tool Suno, with no AI disclosure on Steam.
Creator Edmund McMillen said he had no idea, and publisher Nicalis pulled the files in a patch days later. Recent Steam reviews sit at 8% positive.

paragraphs.text: An update to The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ released on November 19, 2026 included music that players traced to the AI music generator Suno, and publisher Nicalis removed the files in a patch after a backlash, according to GamesRadar+, PC Gamer and ShiftDelete.Net.

The update brought Repentance+ to PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X and S. It also added a secret daily run called Crime Mode, a parody of Grand Theft Auto with a wanted rating, guns and police, released on the same day as GTA 6, PC Gamer reported.
How players found the AI music

Players first noticed that the Crime Mode music sounded machine-made. A user on the game's subreddit then examined the music files and found Suno metadata in the file comments, according to PC Gamer. Power Up Gaming reported that players found seven full songs plus extra intros and outros, with some files tagged as made with Suno and one timestamped October 30, 2026.

The game's Steam store page carried no AI-generated content disclosure, even though Valve's rules ask developers to disclose AI-generated content, including sound, ShiftDelete.Net and Power Up Gaming noted. None of the reports identified who made or added the tracks, and GamesRadar+ said there was no word yet on how they got into the game.
The response from McMillen and Nicalis

Edmund McMillen, the game's original creator and lead designer, wrote on X that he had no idea the daily run featured generated music and that he was looking into how it happened and getting it removed. PC Gamer noted that Nicalis licenses the game from its creator and that many players blamed the publisher.

Nicalis released a patch on PC that removed the generated music files and also fixed bugs, improved netcode and restored compatibility for mods. The patch was submitted to Microsoft, Nintendo and Sony, with no console release date given, according to GamesRadar+ and ShiftDelete.Net.

Steam showed recent reviews for Repentance+ as Overwhelmingly Negative on November 23, with 8% of 1,205 reviews from the previous 30 days positive. Overall reviews stood at Mixed, at 50% positive. Reviews quoted by the outlets also complained about new bugs in the update.

The episode shows how quickly players now check for generated assets, and how little it takes to find them when tool metadata is left in the files. It also shows that a disclosure rule on a store page is only as reliable as the studio filling it in, since the AI music was found by players rather than reported by the developer.
Watch whether Nicalis explains how the tracks were added, whether the console patch ships, and whether Valve acts on the missing AI disclosure on the Repentance+ store page.
